COVID-19 Case Study

Sung Cho

Etienne Lee

Leo Li

1 Background

The outbreak of the novel Corona virus disease 2019 (COVID-19) was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO) on January 30, 2020. Upwards of 755 million cases have been confirmed worldwide, with nearly 6.8 million associated deaths by Feb of 2023. Within the US alone, there have been over 1.1 million deaths and upwards of 102 million cases reported by Feb of 2023. Governments around the world have implemented and suggested a number of policies to lessen the spread of the pandemic, including mask-wearing requirements, travel restrictions, business and school closures, and even stay-at-home orders. The global pandemic has impacted the lives of individuals in countless ways, and though many countries have begun vaccinating individuals, the long-term impact of the virus remains unclear.

The impact of COVID-19 on a given segment of the population appears to vary drastically based on the socioeconomic characteristics of the segment. In particular, differing rates of infection and fatalities have been reported among different racial groups, age groups, and socioeconomic groups. One of the most important metrics for determining the impact of the pandemic is the death rate, which is the proportion of people within the total population that die due to the the disease.

We assembled this dataset for our research with the goal of investigating the effectiveness of lockdowns in flattening the COVID curve. We are providing a portion of the cleaned dataset for this case study.

There are two main goals for this case study:

1.We aim to show the dynamic evolution of COVID cases and COVID-related deaths at the state level.

  1. We aim to identify county-level demographic and policy interventions that are associated with mortality rates in the US. We will construct models to find possible factors related to county-level COVID-19 mortality rates.

  2. This is a rather complex project, but with our team’s help, we have made your job easier.

  3. Please hide all unnecessary lengthy R-output and keep your write-up neat and readable.

Remark1: The data and the statistics reported here were collected before February of 2021.

Remark 2: A group of RAs spent tremendous amount of time working together to assemble the data. It requires data wrangling skills.

2 Data Summary

The data comes from several different sources:

  1. County-level infection and fatality data - This dataset gives daily cumulative numbers on infection and fatality for each county.
    • NYC data
  2. County-level socioeconomic data - The following are the four relevant datasets from this site.
    1. Income - Poverty level and household income.
    2. Jobs - Employment type, rate, and change.
    3. People - Population size, density, education level, race, age, household size, and migration rates.
    4. County Classifications - Type of county (rural or urban on a rural-urban continuum scale).
  3. Intervention Policy Data - This dataset is a manually compiled list of the dates that interventions/lockdown policies were implemented and lifted at the county level.

3 EDA

In this case study, we use the following three nearly cleaned data:

  • covid_county.csv: County-level socialeconomic information that combines the above-mentioned 4 datasets: Income (Poverty level and household income), Jobs (Employment type, rate, and change), People (Population size, density, education level, race, age, household size, and migration rates), County Classifications
  • covid_rates.csv: Daily cumulative numbers on infection and fatality for each county
  • covid_intervention.csv: County-level lockdown intervention.

Among all data, the unique identifier of county is FIPS.

The cleaning procedure is attached in Appendix 2: Data cleaning You may go through it if you are interested or would like to make any changes.

It may need more data wrangling.

3.2 COVID case trend

It is crucial to decide the right granularity for visualization and analysis. We will compare daily vs weekly total new cases by state and we will see it is hard to interpret daily report.

  1. Plot new COVID cases in NY, WA and FL by state and by day. Any irregular pattern? What is the biggest problem of using single day data?

Answer: The daily new case plots for New York, Washington, and Florida show a lot of short-term volatility rather than smooth, consistent trends. There are frequent spikes and dips from one day to the next, many of which don’t seem to reflect actual changes in disease spread. Instead, the patterns suggest irregular reporting, where low counts on certain days are followed by sudden jumps. The main problem with relying on single-day data is that it is noisy and highly sensitive to reporting practices. Factors like weekend reporting delays, testing backlogs, and administrative batching can distort the data, making it hard to interpret real trends. Because of this, daily figures can be misleading, and it is generally more reliable to look at smoothed measures like 7-day averages to understand the underlying trajectory.

  1. Create weekly new cases per 100k weekly_case_per100k. Plot the spaghetti plots of weekly_case_per100k by state. Use TotalPopEst2019 as population.

  1. Summarize the COVID case trend among states based on the plot in ii). What could be the possible reasons to explain the variabilities?
## # A tibble: 10 × 3
##    State        peak_weekly_case_per100k avg_weekly_case_per100k
##    <chr>                           <dbl>                   <dbl>
##  1 North Dakota                    1269.                    261.
##  2 South Dakota                    1153.                    253.
##  3 Iowa                            1036.                    210.
##  4 Arizona                          999.                    198.
##  5 New Jersey                       997.                    169.
##  6 Wyoming                          955.                    186.
##  7 Tennessee                        930.                    213.
##  8 Nebraska                         857.                    195.
##  9 Wisconsin                        835.                    191.
## 10 Minnesota                        831.                    166.

Answer: The plot shows that COVID case trends across states follow a broadly similar pattern—an initial surge in the spring, a relative slowdown in the summer for many states, and then a much larger, more widespread spike in the fall and winter. However, there is substantial variation in both the timing and magnitude of these waves. For example, states like New York experienced a sharp early peak, while others, particularly in the Midwest and South, saw their largest surges later in the year. These differences can be explained by several factors. Population density and urbanization likely played a major role early on, with dense states seeing faster initial spread. Policy responses—such as lockdown timing, mask mandates, and reopening strategies—also varied across states and influenced transmission dynamics. Additionally, behavioral differences, mobility patterns, and even seasonal factors (like people moving indoors in colder months) likely contributed to the variation in case trajectories.

3.3 COVID death trend

In this section, you will use the modern spatial workflow in R (sf + ggplot2) to visualize COVID outcomes.

Important: Do not use usmap for this part. The goal is to become comfortable working directly with sf objects and geom_sf().

By doing so, you will:

  • Become comfortable working with sf objects.
  • Practice spatial joins between geometry and tabular data.
  • Use geom_sf() within the ggplot2 grammar.
  • Understand how geographic resolution affects interpretation.

3.3.1 State-Level Choropleths (2020)

Using sf state geometries:

  • Obtain U.S. state boundaries as an sf object.
  • Join your state-level monthly COVID data to the spatial object.
  • Create one faceted choropleth showing monthly deaths per 100k for each month of 2020.
  • Use a fixed color scale across months so visual comparisons are meaningful.
  • Exclude Alaska and Hawaii if desired.

Hints:

  • Use geom_sf() for mapping.
  • Use facet_wrap(~month) for the 12 panels.
  • Set limits = inside scale_fill_gradient() (or similar) to fix the scale.
  • Extract month/year using lubridate::month() and lubridate::year().

Deliverable: One faceted state-level choropleth figure.

3.3.2 County-Level Choropleth

Now extend the analysis to a finer geographic resolution.

  • Obtain county boundaries as an sf object.
  • Join county-level COVID outcomes (e.g., cumulative 2020 deaths per 100k).
  • Produce a county-level choropleth using geom_sf().

Keep the map visually clean (e.g., suppress county borders if cluttered).

If you compute any distances or spatial quantities, project to a CRS in meters.

Deliverable: One county-level choropleth.

3.3.3 Brief Interpretation (Conceptual)

In 3–5 sentences, briefly discuss:

  • What spatial patterns do you observe?
  • Do you see regional clustering?
  • How does the county map differ from the state map in terms of information revealed?

Answer: There are clear spatial patterns and regional clustering in COVID deaths. Early in the year, higher death rates are concentrated in the Northeast (especially New York and surrounding states), while later months show stronger intensity shifting toward the Midwest and parts of the South. This suggests the pandemic moved in waves across regions rather than affecting all areas uniformly at the same time. Yes, there is evident regional clustering: neighboring states tend to exhibit similar intensity levels, especially during peak periods (e.g., Midwest cluster in fall/winter). This reflects geographic spread and shared regional dynamics such as mobility and policy environments. The county-level map reveals much more granular heterogeneity compared to the state map. While the state map smooths variation and can mask within-state differences, the county map shows localized hotspots and sharp disparities (e.g., specific counties with extremely high death rates within otherwise moderate states). This highlights that aggregation at the state level can obscure important local patterns.

4 COVID factor

We now try to build a good parsimonious model to find possible factors related to death rate on county level. Let us not take time series into account for the moment and use the total number as of March 1, 2021.

  1. Create the response variable total_death_per100k as the total of number of COVID deaths per 100k by March 1, 2021. We suggest to take log transformation as log_total_death_per100k = log(total_death_per100k + 1). Merge total_death_per100k to county_data for the following analysis.

  2. Select possible variables in county_data as covariates. We provide county_data_sub, a subset variables from county_data, for you to get started. Please add any potential variables as you wish.

    1. Report missing values in your final subset of variables.

    2. In the following anaylsis, you may ignore the missing values.

A number of variables contain missing values, though none are critically sparse, the most affected variable (HiAmenity) is missing only 172 out of 3,279 counties. After removing all rows with any missing values, we retain 3,105 counties for the following analysis.

  1. Use LASSO to choose a parsimonious model with all available sensible county-level information. Force in State in the process. Why we need to force in State? You may use lambda.1se to choose a smaller model.

State is forced into the model to control for state-level confounders such as differing policy responses, healthcare infrastructure, and reporting practices. Without controlling for State, these effects would be absorbed into the county-level coefficients and bias our estimates. We select lambda.1se which yields a simpler model with ~63 non-zero coefficients while not sacrificing much predictive performance compared to lambda.min.

  1. Use a quick backward elimination to fine tune the LASSO model from iii). Again force in State in the process.

  2. If necessary, reduce the model from iv) to a final model with all variables being significant at 0.05 level. Are the linear model assumptions all reasonably met?

The residuals vs fitted plot shows reasonably random scatter around zero, with no strong systematic pattern. However, a diagonal line of points at the bottom reflects counties with zero COVID deaths, since these counties all have the same response value of 0, the model cannot distinguish between them based on their predictors, resulting in a cluster of large negative residuals. These same counties likely drive the heavy left tail observed in the Q-Q plot. Overall, though not perfect, the linear model assumptions are reasonably met.

  1. It has been shown that COVID affects elderly the most. It is also claimed that the COVID death rate among African Americans and Latinos is higher. Does your analysis support these arguments?
##                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
## Age65AndOlderPct2010  0.03559    0.00720    4.94 8.11e-07
## HispanicPct2010       0.00761    0.00199    3.83 1.31e-04

Our analysis partially supports these claims. The coefficient for Age65AndOlderPct2010 is positive and highly significant (0.036, p < 0.001), corresponding to a 3.6% increase in county death rate per additional percentage point of elderly population, strongly supporting the claim that COVID disproportionately affects the elderly. HispanicPct2010 is also positive and significant (0.008, p < 0.001), supporting the claim for Latino communities, potentially reflecting higher exposure risk due to essential worker roles and larger household sizes. However, BlackNonHispanicPct2010 was zeroed out by LASSO, suggesting that after controlling for state effects and socioeconomic factors such as income and poverty, Black population percentage does not add additional explanatory power, implying the disparity may be driven more by socioeconomic conditions than race itself.

  1. Based on your final model, summarize your findings. In particular, summarize the state effect controlling for others. Provide intervention recommendations to policy makers to reduce COVID death rate.

Our final model explains 37% of the variance in county-level COVID death rates (adjusted R² = 0.36). Among the most significant county-level predictors, higher agricultural employment (PctEmpAgriculture) and faster natural population growth (NaturalChangeRate1019) were strongly associated with lower death rates, likely reflecting younger and healthier rural populations. Conversely, higher proportions of elderly residents (Age65AndOlderPct2010) were associated with higher death rates, consistent with the well-known vulnerability of older populations to COVID-19. The positive effect of youth population (Under18Pct2010) is more surprising, and may reflect that counties with more children tend to have larger household sizes, facilitating spread to vulnerable adults.

Controlling for these county-level factors, there remain significant state-level differences in death rates. States with the lowest death rates relative to Alabama include Vermont, Maine, Utah, Oregon, and Washington, predominantly New England and Pacific Northwest states known for early and strict public health interventions. In contrast, North Dakota and South Dakota had significantly higher death rates, consistent with their well-documented resistance to lockdown measures early in the pandemic.

Based on these findings, we recommend that policymakers prioritize early implementation of lockdowns and mask mandates, particularly in states with resistance to such measures. Additional targeted interventions should focus on counties with high elderly populations and low income levels, as these appear to be the most vulnerable.

  1. What else can we do to improve our model? What other important information we may have missed?

Several improvements could be made to this model. First, counties with zero reported deaths may reflect unreported cases rather than true zeros, distorting the model as seen in the residual plot — these could be handled by dropping them entirely or using a more appropriate transformation. Second, rather than dropping the 174 counties with missing values via na.omit(), imputing missing values via softImpute as suggested in part ix) could recover useful data and improve model stability.

More importantly, several key variables likely explaining much of the remaining 63% unexplained variance are absent from our data. Vaccination rates, hospital capacity and healthcare access, mask mandate compliance, mobility patterns, and county-level comorbidity rates such as obesity and diabetes are all strongly linked to COVID severity but were unavailable at the county level at the time of data collection. Including these variables would likely substantially improve the model’s explanatory power.

  1. (Optional) Would your findings be very different if you had refined the data in some way or imputed the missing values in part ii). Check PCA lecture, section 10 for imputations via softImpute.

5 Executive summary

Please summarize this project as follows (no more than one page):

  • Goal of the study

  • Data

    • Source and a brief description of the data
    • How do you assemble them together (mostly done by our team but you may present them as if you have done so)

  • Analyses

  • Methods used

  • Findings

  • Limitations

Goal

This study has two main goals: to visualize the dynamic evolution of COVID-19 cases and deaths at the state level over time, and to identify county-level demographic and socioeconomic factors associated with COVID-19 mortality rates across the United States.

Data

Data was assembled from three sources:

  • NYT GitHub Repository: County-level daily COVID-19 infection and fatality counts
  • USDA Economic Research Service: County-level socioeconomic data covering income, employment, education, population, and county classifications
  • Intervention Policy Data: County-level lockdown and intervention dates

Assembling these datasets required substantial data wrangling, NYC borough-level data was extracted and reformatted separately, all datasets were merged using FIPS codes as the unique county identifier, cumulative death and case counts were computed from raw daily figures, and population estimates were joined to enable per-100k normalization.

Analyses

  • EDA: Spaghetti plots of weekly cases per 100k and choropleth maps of monthly deaths per 100k at both state and county level, built using the sf and ggplot2 spatial workflow
  • Modeling: LASSO regression with 10-fold cross-validation to select county-level predictors of log COVID death rate per 100k as of March 1, 2021, with State forced in as a control variable, followed by backward elimination via stepAIC and removal of remaining insignificant variables at the 0.05 level

Findings

COVID cases followed broadly similar wave patterns across states, with an early surge in the Northeast, a relative slowdown in summer, and a much larger wave in fall and winter. State and county choropleth maps confirmed regional clustering, with deaths concentrated in the Northeast early and shifting toward the Midwest and South later in the year.

At the county level, our final model (adjusted R² = 0.36) identified the following key factors:

  • Increases death rate: Higher elderly population, higher youth population, higher Hispanic population, higher manufacturing employment
  • Decreases death rate: Higher income, agricultural employment, education levels, natural population growth

Controlling for county-level factors, states in New England and the Pacific Northwest such as Vermont, Maine, Oregon and Washington had significantly lower death rates, consistent with their early and strict public health interventions, while Great Plains states such as North Dakota and South Dakota had significantly higher death rates, consistent with their resistance to lockdown measures. We therefore recommend that policymakers prioritize early lockdowns and mask mandates, with targeted support for counties with high elderly populations and low income levels.

Limitations

  • The data cuts off at March 1, 2021, predating widespread vaccination and not capturing the full pandemic trajectory
  • Counties with zero reported deaths may reflect underreporting rather than true zeros, distorting model estimates
  • Missing values in 39 variables required dropping 174 counties via listwise deletion rather than imputation
  • Key predictors unavailable at the county level include vaccination rates, hospital capacity, mask mandate compliance, and comorbidity rates such as obesity and diabetes, which likely explain much of the remaining unexplained variance

8 Appendix 2: Data cleaning

The raw data sets are dirty and need transforming before we can do our EDA. It takes time and efforts to clean and merge different data sources so we provide the final output of the cleaned and merged data. The cleaning procedure is as follows. Please read through to understand what is in the cleaned data. We set eval = data_cleaned in the following cleaning chunks so that these cleaning chunks will only run if any of data/covid_county.csv, data/covid_rates.csv or data/covid_intervention.csv does not exist.

We first read in the table using data.table::fread(), as we did last time.

8.1 Clean NYC data

The original NYC data contains more information than we need. We extract only the number of cases and deaths and format it the same as the covid_rates data.

8.2 Continental US cases

We only consider cases and death in continental US. Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico have 02, 15, and 72 as their respective first 2 digits of their FIPS. We use the %/% operator for integer division to get the first 2 digits of FIPS. We also remove Virgin Islands and Northern Mariana Islands. All data of counties in NYC are aggregated as County == "New York City" in covid_rates with no FIPS, so we combine the NYC data into covid_rate.

8.3 COVID date to week

We set the week of Jan 21, 2020 (the first case of COVID case in US) as the first week (2020-01-19 to 2020-01-25).

8.4 COVID infection/mortality rates

Merge the TotalPopEst2019 variable from the demographic data with covid_rates by FIPS.

8.5 NA in COVID data

NA values in the covid_rates data set correspond to a county not having confirmed cases/deaths. We replace the NA values in these columns with zeros. FIPS for Kansas city, Missouri, Rhode Island and some others are missing. We drop them for the moment and output the data up to week 57 as covid_rates.csv.

8.6 Formatting date in int_dates

We convert the columns representing dates in int_dates to R Date types using as.Date(). We will need to specify that the origin parameter is "0001-01-01". We output the data as covid_intervention.csv.

8.7 Merge demographic data

Merge the demographic data sets by FIPS and output as covid_county.csv.
